analysis.one_liner: Bans manipulative design features and disguised advertising on online platforms aimed at children under 16.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2020 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The KIDS Act would outlaw design tricks on child-directed online platforms that keep kids scrolling: autoplay that queues the next video, push alerts nudging kids back to the app, engagement badges, and features that push kids to spend money. It would ban advertising to children that disguises itself as entertainment — influencer pitches, product placement, host-selling — and bar ads for alcohol, nicotine, and tobacco on these platforms. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, audit the 25 largest child-directed platforms annually, label content for parents, and fund grants for ad-free educational children's content.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 16 who use commercial websites, apps, and video platforms, and their parents. The bill's own findings describe children as uniquely susceptible to manipulation because the brain systems needed to resist it develop later. Parents would gain a labeling system to identify noncommercial, educational content, and creators of ad-free children's content could win federal grants.

how_it_helps.text: Bars child-directed platforms from using autoplay, push alerts, engagement badges, and other features that push kids to spend more time or money on the platform.

Prohibits disguised advertising to children, including host-selling, program-length ads, native advertising, branded content, and product placement, and bans ads or heavily commercial content involving alcohol, nicotine, or tobacco.
Bars amplification of content involving sexual material, violence, bullying, gambling, or other dangerous or exploitative material, and requires a mechanism for users to report violations.
Requires annual FTC audits of the 25 child-directed platforms with the most child users and public reports to Congress on their compliance.
Creates a Commerce Department grant program for advertisement-free, educational online content for children, authorized at $4 million in 2021 rising to $12 million in 2024.

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, the cost would fall on commercial online platforms that reach children — video sites, social media, and app operators — through lost ad revenue, compliance costs, and FTC fines, and on advertisers who would lose access to child audiences. Taxpayers would fund the grant program.

drawbacks.text: By cutting ad revenue and engagement-driven growth on free child-directed platforms, the bill could push those services toward paid subscriptions or reduce the free content available to families.

The ban on 'amplifying' a wide range of content — including vaguely defined 'wholly commercial' or 'dangerous' material — gives platforms an incentive to over-restrict, and the definition of what counts as 'directed to children' would sweep in platforms with mixed-age audiences.

Compliance and FTC rulemaking would impose real costs, and the bill's revenue authorization ($34 million for grants over four years) covers grants but not the full audit and enforcement workload placed on the FTC.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are aimed at a real, documented problem — engagement-maximizing design and disguised advertising directed at children — and the costs fall mostly on platforms and advertisers rather than on families. The main trade-off is that rules written against 'manipulative' design are inherently fuzzy, which risks both over-blocking by platforms and litigation over what counts as child-directed content.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Kathy Castor of Florida introduced the KIDS Act on September 24, 2020, with Representatives Yvette Clarke and Jennifer Wexton.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
No further action was taken; the bill received only two cosponsors and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the committee acting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online platforms and advertisers that target children kept their existing practices — autoplay, engagement nudges, and disguised advertising — because the bill never advanced. Families and children gained nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the KIDS Act to ban manipulative design features and disguised advertising on child-directed platforms.

for.name: Reps. Yvette Clarke and Jennifer Wexton
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only two cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 24, 2020 and took no action on it — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only three Democratic sponsors and no recorded opposition or votes, so no partisan pattern can be measured from the record; it simply never moved past referral.

industries.industry: Online platforms and video/social apps serving children
industries.note: The bill would outlaw the engagement features (autoplay, push alerts, badges) and ad formats (native ads, influencer marketing, product placement) that drive these platforms' child-audience revenue, and subject the largest 25 to annual FTC audits. Their financial interest lay in the bill not advancing.
The bill would ban most disguised advertising formats directed at children, cutting off a segment of ad spending that works by blurring the line between entertainment and selling.

industries.industry: Creators of educational, ad-free children's content
industries.note: A federal grant program (up to $12 million a year by 2024) would fund and promote advertisement-free, educational online content for children.
